title: Breakthrough
summary: Create a passed pawn by sacrificing one or two pawns, after counting whether the enemy king can catch it.
part.classic.title: Classic breakthrough
part.classic.summary: Three pawns against three, with the kings far away. The middle pawn is sacrificed, its neighbour deflects the pawn guarding the file, and the third one queens.
part.count.title: Count first
part.count.summary: Before sacrificing, count whether the enemy king catches the new passed pawn. If it does, improve the position first, as Capablanca should have done against Lasker.
part.kingInstead.title: When the break fails
part.kingInstead.summary: With the enemy king close to the pawns, the breakthrough does not work yet. Bring your own king first and only then break through.
part.order.title: Fix before you break
part.order.summary: Of two advances that look alike, the one that makes contact first gets the passed pawn born one square further up.
part.side.title: Far from the king
part.side.summary: Choose the advance that creates the passed pawn far from the enemy king, on the side where it is not.
part.secondPasser.title: The second passed pawn
part.secondPasser.summary: A king watching one passed pawn cannot watch another. A breakthrough on the other wing creates the second one, far from it.
part.pushPast.title: Pass, don't trade
part.pushPast.summary: With the pawns in contact, capturing or swapping looks natural and often loses. Capablanca beat Lasker by pushing one more pawn into contact without capturing.
part.kingFirst.title: King first
part.kingFirst.summary: If the opponent has a passed pawn too, both sides queen and it is a draw. Put your king in front of their pawn before you break through.
part.defense.title: The defence
part.defense.summary: When defending with the move, push the middle pawn into contact before the breakthrough and recapture with the pawn on the right side.
part.defenseKing.title: With the king close
part.defenseKing.summary: Without the middle pawn, make contact from the edge and bring the king in front of whichever pawn is left.
part.finish.title: Summary
part.finish.summary: The three rules of the breakthrough, the defence seen from the other side, and a practical challenge to finish.
step.t_classic: Three pawns against three, face to face, and both kings far away. No pawn is passed, and the black king can't help. Can White get a pawn to the eighth rank?
step.t_classic.hint1: One pawn alone can't get past three. But if you give away one or two pawns, the black pawns must capture and step out of the way; and if they don't capture, the pawn that advanced captures and queens.
step.t_classic.hint2: Which pawn, when it advances, threatens two black pawns at the same time?
step.classicWhy: 1.b6! It threatens 2.bxa7 and 2.bxc7, with a queen right after, so Black has to capture. Whether Black takes with the a-pawn or the c-pawn, one file is left unguarded in front of a pawn of mine, and the other pawn sacrifices itself to deflect whoever still guards that file. Watch the capture with the a-pawn first.
step.d_classic: Black took with the a-pawn. The a-file is free in front of my a5-pawn; only the b7-pawn still guards a6. Watch the second sacrifice.
step.d_classic.m1: 1.c6! Another pawn given away, on purpose. It threatens 2.cxb7 and, if Black doesn't take, it reaches c8.
step.d_classic.m2: Black takes. The b7-pawn has left the b-file, and it was the one guarding a6.
step.d_classic.m3: 2.a6. No black pawn can touch this pawn. Two moves to the queen.
step.d_classic.m4: The black king runs. To catch the pawn, it would have to reach b7 before the promotion.
step.d_classic.m5: 3.a7. One square from the queen. The black king would have to be on b7 right now, and it is on f7: the queen comes next move. Notice the black pawns on b6 and c6, a long way from the first rank.
step.otherCapture: And if Black takes with the c-pawn? It's the mirror image. Now the c-file has no black pawn in front of my c5-pawn, and only the b7-pawn guards c6. The second sacrifice is 1.a6!, to deflect that pawn. After the first sacrifice, look at which file became free: that file's pawn is the one that will get through.
step.classicMove: Your turn. Black took with the c-pawn.
step.classicMove.hint: The c-file is free in front of your c5-pawn. Who guards c6? Deflect that pawn.
step.classicMove.done: That's it. 1.a6 deflected the b7-pawn, and the c-pawn went straight through. Only that path won.
step.t_count: Same idea, but now the black king is on e8, closer. White has already taken the pawn to b6 and Black took with the a-pawn. Does the breakthrough still work? Count before you play.
step.t_count.hint1: Play the breakthrough in your head to the end: 1.c6 bxc6 2.a6. Now it's Black's move. Where must the king get to in order to stop the a6-pawn?
step.t_count.hint2: The a6-pawn queens in two moves. The black king has to reach b7 first. Count the king moves from e8, remembering that c7 is taken by a black pawn.
step.square: It's a count of moves. After 1.c6 bxc6 and 2.a6, the pawn is two squares from queening, and Black is to move. The king on e8 needs three moves to reach b7: d8, c8, b7. The pawn needs two. The king is too late, and the breakthrough works. One move less, and it would fail.
step.capaCount: Even masters get this count wrong. {{London|london}}, 1913: {{José Raúl Capablanca|jose-raul-capablanca}}, who would become world champion eight years later, was playing a friendly game against {{Edward Lasker|edward-lasker}}. Only kings and pawns were left, and Capablanca wanted to create a passed pawn on the kingside. He played 39.f5?, and after 39...gxf5 40.h5 the black king could come back with 40...Ke6 and hold: the breakthrough came too early. The right way was to prepare with 39.a3!, keeping a4 in reserve for the moment the black king ran out of good squares, and only then break with f5 and h5. Count before you break; if the count does not work, improve the position first.
step.countMove: Back to the king on e8. Make the breakthrough and take the pawn to the seventh rank.
step.countMove.hint: You've already counted: the king on e8 arrives late. Deflect the b7-pawn and run with the a-pawn.
step.countMove.done: That's it. The black king went to d7, but the pawn is already on a7 and queens next move.
step.t_tooClose: Three pawns against two, b5, c5 and d5 against c7 and d7, and the black king on d8, right on top of them; your king is on g1. You are a pawn up. Does the breakthrough work now, or is there a better plan?
step.t_tooClose.hint1: Play 1.b6 in your head: 1...cxb6 2.cxb6, and the new pawn is born on b6, next to the king on d8. Do the same count with 1.c6 and with 1.d6.
step.t_tooClose.hint2: A pawn given is a pawn gone. A pawn up, you don't need to give anything now: which piece of yours hasn't joined the game yet?
step.tooClose: Here any breakthrough, 1.b6, 1.c6 or 1.d6, only draws: the new pawn is born next to the king on d8, and the king catches it. But a pawn up, I don't need to give anything now. The plan is to bring the king, 1.Kf2, 2.Ke3, 3.Kd4, and only then break, with the king alongside to support the new pawn. When the count says the enemy king gets there, keep the breakthrough for later and bring your own king.
step.d_tooClose: The king has reached c4, next to the pawns. Now the same breakthrough that only drew wins, because the new pawn has someone to protect it. Watch.
step.d_tooClose.m1: 1.b6! Now it works. The pawn about to be born on b6 will have the king on c4 one move away.
step.d_tooClose.m2: Black takes. If 1...Kc8, 2.bxc7 Kxc7 and two connected pawns, c5 and d5, are left with my king alongside: they win.
step.d_tooClose.m3: 2.cxb6. The new pawn is born on b6, as before; only before my king was on g1, and now it is on c4.
step.d_tooClose.m4: The black king goes to c8, from where it watches b7. On its own, the b6-pawn would not get through.
step.d_tooClose.m5: 3.Kc5. The king protects the b6-pawn and eyes d6: the black d7-pawn is left without a defender.
step.d_tooClose.m6: The black king leans on the b6-pawn. That is all it can do.
step.d_tooClose.m7: 4.Kd6. The king steps in: if 4...Kxb6, 5.Kxd7 and the d-pawn queens; if the king stays, 5.Kxd7 all the same. With the king close, the breakthrough turned into a win.
step.tooCloseMove: Your turn, back to the king on g1. Don't give any pawn now.
step.tooCloseMove.hint: Any breakthrough draws: the king on d8 catches the new pawn. Start bringing the king, on its way to d4.
step.tooCloseMove.done: That's it. The king comes, and the pawns wait. With it on d4 or c4, the breakthrough that only drew starts to win.
step.t_order: Two pawns against one on the queenside, b4 and c4 against b6, and the black king far away on g5, with its g6-pawn. The two advances, 1.b5 and 1.c5, look alike. Only one wins. Which, and why?
step.t_order.hint1: After the breakthrough, Black is left with a passed pawn too. Count both races to the last rank.
step.t_order.hint2: One of the advances lets your new pawn be born a square closer to b8.
step.orderWhy: 1.b5! Fix first: the b6-pawn is pinned down, with my b5-pawn in contact with it. Now 2.c5 comes with force: 2...bxc5 3.b6, and the passed pawn is already born on b6, two moves from the queen. The black c5-pawn needs three moves to reach c2 and one more to queen. Mine gets there first, and the new queen stops the c-pawn.
step.orderWrong: In the wrong order, 1.c5? bxc5 2.b5, the passed pawn is born on b5, not b6: one move behind. Watch the race from Black's side.
step.orderWrong.m1: 2...c4. The black pawn runs at once: three squares to go, c3, c2 and c1.
step.orderWrong.m2: 3.b6. The white pawn still needs b7 and b8.
step.orderWrong.m3: 3...c3. Now both pawns are two squares from a queen.
step.orderWrong.m4: 4.b7. One move from a queen, but Black is too.
step.orderWrong.m5: 4...c2. Both pawns queen on the same move.
step.orderWrong.m6: 5.b8=Q. The white queen is born first, but it doesn't stop the c2-pawn.
step.orderWrong.m7: 5...c1=Q+. The black queen is born with check: queen against queen, a draw. One square less for the white pawn, and the win is gone.
step.orderMove: Your turn, from the same position. Fix first, then break.
step.orderMove.hint: Which advance lets your new pawn be born a square further up? Make contact with the b6-pawn before you give up the c-pawn.
step.orderMove.done: That's it. 1.b5 fixed the b6-pawn, 2.c5 deflected it, and the passed pawn was already born on b6: it queens before Black's c-pawn.
step.t_side: Different pawns: White on c5 and e5, Black on d7, e7 and d6. The black king is on h8. There's a breakthrough here. With which pawn?
step.t_side.hint1: Try both advances, 1.c6 and 1.e6. After each one, a black pawn captures. Which white pawn is left with a free file?
step.t_side.hint2: One of the advances leaves the e5-pawn still blocked by the e7-pawn. The other frees a pawn on a file far from the black king.
step.sideWhy: 1.e6! It threatens 2.exd7 and queening. If the d7-pawn takes, the c5-pawn has nobody in front or beside it: c6, c7, c8. And the black king on h8 is on the other side of the board. 1.c6? is no use: the e5-pawn would still be blocked by the e7-pawn. That's what changes from the classic: here there is no middle pawn to sacrifice, and the right advance is the one that frees a pawn on a file far from the king.
step.d_side: Now the mirror image: black pawns on c7, d7 and d6, and the black king on a8, close to the c-file. 1.e6 would not win here: the c-pawn would be born next to the king. The breakthrough is on the other side.
step.d_side.m1: 1.c6! It threatens 2.cxd7 and queening on d8: Black has to capture.
step.d_side.m2: Black takes, and the e7-pawn has left the e-file: it is free in front of my pawn.
step.d_side.m3: 2.e6. Nobody can touch this pawn, and the black king is at the far end.
step.d_side.m4: The black king comes, but from b7 it can't reach d7 or e8 in time.
step.d_side.m5: 3.e7. One square from the queen; the king would have to be on d7 or e8 right now, and it is on b7. The queen comes next move.
step.t_twoPassers: In the previous chapter the new pawn was born far from the king; here the black king is already tied to the a6-pawn: if it walks away, a7 and a8. On the other side, e4 and f4 against f6, and Black still has the h5-pawn. What's the move?
step.t_twoPassers.hint1: Does your king on a1 catch the h-pawn? Count.
step.t_twoPassers.hint2: Which advance creates the second passer with a threat, without giving the h-pawn time?
step.twoPassers: 1.e5! threatens 2.exf6, and the f6-pawn has to take. 1.f5? looks the same, but threatens nothing, and 1...h4! gets there first.
step.d_twoPassers: The black king can't leave the a6-pawn, and the h-pawn is already running. I break now.
step.d_twoPassers.m1: 1.e5! I give the e-pawn with a threat: if Black doesn't take, 2.exf6 and the f-pawn gets through.
step.d_twoPassers.m2: 1...fxe5. The f-file is open: my f4-pawn has nobody in front of it any more.
step.d_twoPassers.m3: 2.f5. The second passed pawn is born, far from the black king, which is still tied to the a6-pawn.
step.d_twoPassers.m4: 2...h4. The h-pawn runs: my king on a1 can't catch it.
step.d_twoPassers.m6: 3...h3. The h-pawn is two moves from a queen too.
step.d_twoPassers.m7: 4.f7. Next move, 5.f8=Q comes with check to the king on a8, one move before the black queen: 4...h2 5.f8=Q+, and White wins.
step.twoPassersMove: Your turn, from the same position. Create the second passed pawn before the h-pawn arrives.
step.twoPassersMove.hint: The winning advance comes with a threat. The other one lets the h-pawn run for free.
step.twoPassersMove.done: That's it. 1.e5 forced the f6-pawn off its file, the f-pawn ran and the white queen is born first, with check. The king on a8, tied to the a6-pawn, could do nothing.
step.sideMove: Back to the king on h8.
step.sideMove.hint: Advance the pawn that forces the d7-pawn to capture and frees the pawn on the file far from the king.
step.sideMove.done: That's it. 1.e6 pulled the d7-pawn out of the way, and the c-pawn went alone to c7. The black king never came close.
step.t_push: Back to {{Capablanca|jose-raul-capablanca}} against {{Lasker|edward-lasker}}, two moves later. Capablanca did break with 39.f5 and 40.h5, and Lasker answered 40...Ke5, with his king close to the pawns. The natural move is 41.g6, to swap after 41...hxg6 and follow with 42.h6, clearing the way for the h-pawn. Is it right?
step.t_push.hint1: Play 41.g6 in your head to the end: 41...hxg6, 42.h6, and now the black king goes to f6. Does it reach the h-pawn?
step.t_push.hint2: What if no pawn captured right now? One of yours can walk past the black pawn, and then 42.g6 comes with more force.
step.pushWhy: 41.h6!! {{Capablanca|jose-raul-capablanca}} did not swap: he pushed the h-pawn up against h7. The black king can't even go back to f6, because the g5-pawn covers that square, and 42.g6 comes next move whatever Black does: if 42...hxg6, 43.h7 and a queen; if not, 43.gxh7 and a queen. {{Lasker|edward-lasker}} resigned. 41.g6? first was the mistake: 41...hxg6 42.h6 Kf6, the king reaches the h-pawn, and Black would win with the f- and d-pawns. Contact first, break second: that way one of the two pawns gets through, however Black captures.
step.d_push: The same idea in a composed position: pawns on e6 and f5 against e7 and f7, the black king on h7. Taking on f7 is natural and loses: 1.exf7? Kg7, the king captures the pawn and the e7-pawn decides. Watch the move that passes.
step.d_push.m1: 1.f6! I don't take on f7: I make contact. If 1...exf6, 2.e7 and the pawn queens; if 1...fxe6, 2.fxe7 and it queens the other way.
step.d_push.m3: 2.e7. The e6-pawn walked past the f7-pawn without capturing: the f7-pawn only covers e6 and g6, and e7 was free.
step.d_push.m4: The black king runs, but the pawn is already on e7: it arrives one move too late.
step.d_push.m5: Queen. Taking on f7 would have let the king catch the pawn; the winning move was the one that walked past.
step.pushMove: Your turn. Pawns on c5 and d6 against c7 and d7, the black king on a7. Taking on c7 is natural.
step.pushMove.hint: After 1.dxc7, the king goes to b7 and captures the pawn. These are the two central files, not the edge: which pawn makes contact without capturing, and which one walks past?
step.pushMove.done: That's it. 1.c6 made contact without capturing; Black took on c6, the d-file opened and the d6-pawn walked past and queens, far from the king. 1.dxc7?, on the other hand, even lost: 1...Kb7, the king captures the pawn and the d7-pawn decides.
step.t_kingFirst: The 1.f5 breakthrough is ready: 1.f5 gxf5 2.h5 and the h-pawn runs. But Black has the passed b6-pawn, and your king is on a1. Break now?
step.t_kingFirst.hint1: After 1.f5 gxf5 2.h5, count the race to the end: who queens with check?
step.t_kingFirst.hint2: The king has to be inside the square of both black pawns before the breakthrough.
step.kingFirstWhy: 1.f5? gives Black a passed pawn on the f-file, and the king on a1 can't reach it. Watch.
step.d_kingFirstWrong: After 1.f5? gxf5 2.h5, the race from Black's side.
step.d_kingFirstWrong.m1: 2...f4. The pawn that captured on f5 runs: my king on a1 is far away from it.
step.d_kingFirstWrong.m3: 3...f3. Both are two squares from a queen.
step.d_kingFirstWrong.m5: 4...f2. But the black pawn is one move away too.
step.d_kingFirstWrong.m6: 5.h8=Q. The white queen is born first.
step.d_kingFirstWrong.m7: 5...f1=Q+. The black queen is born with check to the king on a1, and the b6-pawn is still on the board: a draw.
step.kingFirstPath: 1.Kb2!, and if 1...b5, 2.Kc3! From c3 the king watches the b-pawn and reaches the f-pawn.
step.kingFirstMove: Your turn. Bring the king first and only then break.
step.kingFirstMove.hint: The king heads for the centre, inside the square of both black pawns; the 1.f5 breakthrough only afterwards.
step.kingFirstMove.done: That's it. The king on c3 watches the b-pawn and reaches the f-pawn, and only then 3.f5 and 4.h5: now it's a race of one pawn only.
step.t_defense: Now you defend. White pawns on f5, g5 and h5 against yours on f7, g7 and h7, and your king on g3, far from the eighth rank. If it were White's move, 1.g6! would be the 1.b6 of the first chapter, and a pawn would get through. But it's your move. How do you take the breakthrough away?
step.t_defense.hint1: Waiting with the king doesn't help: 2.g6 comes. Look for a pawn move that takes the middle sacrifice away from White.
step.t_defense.hint2: One of your three pawns can advance and touch the white pawns. Only one of them holds.
step.defenseWhy: 1...g6! The defender pushes the middle pawn into contact before the attacker does. Now, if White captures, 2.hxg6 or 2.fxg6, the pawns get exchanged and no white pawn gets through; and my pawn on g6 means White's g6 can no longer happen. The other advances, 1...f6 and 1...h6, hand over the breakthrough through the neighbouring pawn: only 1...g6 holds.
step.d_defense: Black played 1...g6 and White took with the f-pawn. Three white pawns, g6, g5 and h5, against mine on f7 and h7. Which pawn do I recapture with? Watch.
step.d_defense.m1: 2...fxg6! I recapture with the pawn on the same side the white pawn came from. That way my h7-pawn stays in front of the h5-pawn.
step.d_defense.m2: 3.hxg6. White exchanges. If 3.h6, the pawns are blocked, g6 against g5 and h7 against h6, and nobody gets through.
step.d_defense.m3: 3...hxg6. One pawn each is left, g5 against g6, blocked. No white pawn gets through.
step.d_defense.m4: The white king can walk as much as it likes: there is no pawn left to support.
step.d_defense.m5: 4...Kf4. My king watches the g5-pawn, and the position goes nowhere: a draw. Had I recaptured 2...hxg6?, 3.h6! and the h-pawn would get through.
step.defenseMove: Black has already taken the pawn to g6, and White took with the h-pawn. Which pawn do you recapture with?
step.defenseMove.hint: Recapture with the pawn on the same side the white pawn came from. That way the other white pawn still has a black pawn in front of it.
step.defenseMove.done: That's it. After 2.fxg6 and 2...fxg6, one pawn each is left, blocked: a draw. Had you taken with the f-pawn, 2.f6! would have given White a passed pawn.
step.t_defenseKing: You defend again: three white pawns, a5, b5 and c5, against yours on a7 and b7, and your king on d7, close by. If it were White's move, 1.b6! would break through. Here there is no middle pawn to push into contact. What holds?
step.t_defenseKing.hint1: Waiting with the king loses: 2.b6 comes, and a pawn gets through. Only one pawn move takes the breakthrough away from White.
step.t_defenseKing.hint2: Of the two advances, 1...a6 and 1...b6, one hands over the breakthrough through the neighbouring pawn. Count what White does after each.
step.defenseKing: With the king close, the defence gains a second resource. Here it is three white pawns against two, a5, b5 and c5 against a7 and b7, and your king on d7. There is no middle pawn to push into contact; what holds is 1...a6!, making contact from the side. If 2.bxa6 bxa6, and the a-pawns block each other while your king looks after the c-pawn. If White advances 2.b6, your king goes after the pawns, 2...Kc6!, and the c5-pawn falls. With the king close, the rule is: make contact before the breakthrough and take the king in front of whatever pawn is left.
step.d_defenseKing: Watch first what happens when White exchanges.
step.d_defenseKing.m1: 1...a6! I make contact from the edge. Now 2.b6 is no breakthrough any more: my king goes to c6 and captures the c5-pawn. And if White captures, I exchange.
step.d_defenseKing.m2: 2.bxa6. The b5-pawn has gone to a6, and my b7-pawn recaptures.
step.d_defenseKing.m3: 2...bxa6. The a-pawns block each other, a5 against a6. The c5-pawn is left, and my king is right beside it.
step.d_defenseKing.m4: The white king comes, but it is much too far.
step.d_defenseKing.m5: 3...Kc6. I attack the c5-pawn, and nobody can defend it.
step.d_defenseKing.m6: The white king reaches e3: still two moves from c5.
step.d_defenseKing.m7: 4...Kxc5. No passed pawn, no win: a draw. I made contact before the breakthrough, and the king went to collect what was left.
step.defenseKingMove: Make contact first, then bring the king.
step.defenseKingMove.hint: The pawn that makes contact is the outside one, there is no middle pawn. Then, if White advances, the king attacks the pawns.
step.defenseKingMove.done: That's it. 1...a6 took the breakthrough away, and the king went to collect the c5-pawn. No passed pawn, no win.
step.recap: Three rules for your games. First: three against three, face to face, the middle pawn is sacrificed first; then its neighbour deflects the guard of the file that became free, and the new pawn is born far from the enemy king.
step.recapCount: Second: before you give the pawn, count. If the enemy king catches the new pawn, bring your own king first, as here, or don't break; if the opponent has a passed pawn too, your king steps in front of it before the breakthrough.
step.recapPush: Third: when the pawns are in contact, fix or pass instead of capturing. The pawn that gets through is the one that does not capture.
step.recapDefense: And the defence is the mirror image. The defender to move pushes a pawn into contact before the breakthrough: the middle one, when there is one; the outside one, when there isn't. Recapture with the pawn on the same side and take the king in front of whatever pawn is left.
step.recapMove: The blow once more, before the game. Black took with the a-pawn.
step.recapMove.hint: The a5-pawn has a free file; only the b7-pawn guards a6.
step.recapMove.done: That's it. 1.c6 deflected the b7-pawn, and the a5-pawn got through.
step.finish: Now the practical challenge. Black has already taken with the a-pawn, and the black king is on f1, far away. Only one move wins. White to move and win: count, and play on to the queen.
ex.e01: Two pawns against one, and the black king on d8. Find the winning move.
ex.e01.hint: The a6-pawn is two squares from queening, but the a7-pawn is in the way. Get it out of the way.
ex.e01.solution: 1.b6! If 1...axb6, 2.a7, and the king on d8 doesn't reach b7 in time. If Black doesn't take, for example with 1...Kc8, 2.bxa7 and the pawn queens. White's king moves only draw.
ex.e08: Three pawns against two, but the black king is on c8, right next to the pawns. Find the winning move.
ex.e08.hint: Count before you sacrifice: after a breakthrough, does the black king catch the new pawn? If it does, look for another plan.
ex.e08.solution: Here the breakthrough only draws: the king on c8 catches the new pawn. With an extra pawn, the plan is to bring the king. Any king move, such as 1.Kf2, wins; 1.a6, 1.b6 or 1.c6 right now throw the win away.
ex.e10: Three white pawns against two, and the black king on d7. What do you do before White plays 2.b6? Find the draw.
ex.e10.hint: Push a pawn into contact with the white pawns to take the breakthrough away, and let the king handle the rest.
ex.e10.solution: 1...a6! After 2.bxa6, the king goes to c8 and, after 3.c6, to b8, in front of the a-pawn. The c7-pawn blocks the c6-pawn. Only 1...a6 draws, and after that only 2...Kc8 and 3...Kb8 hold.
ex.e11: Two pawns against one: b4 and c4 against b6, with the black king on g5 and yours on h1. In what order do the pawns advance? Find the winning move.
ex.e11.hint: The two advances look alike, but one of them leaves the new pawn a square closer to b8. And remember that, after the breakthrough, Black is left with a passed pawn too.
ex.e11.solution: 1.b5! Fix first: after 1...Kf4, 2.c5! bxc5 and 3.b6, the passed pawn is already on b6 and queens before Black's c-pawn. If 1.c5 first, 1...bxc5 2.b5 c4!, and both pawns queen together: a draw. Only 1.b5 wins.
ex.e12: Your pawns on g5 and h6 are in contact with the black pawns on g7 and h7, kings on e5 and e7. Taking on g7 is the natural move. Count first. Find the winning move.
ex.e12.hint: After 1.hxg7, the black king goes to f7 and captures the pawn. Look for a pawn move that leaves the black pawns without a good answer.
ex.e12.solution: 1.g6! If 1...gxh6, 2.gxh7 and the pawn queens on h8; if 1...hxg6, 2.h7 and it queens the same way. But 1.hxg7? loses: 1...Kf7, the king captures the g7-pawn and the a7-pawn decides later. Only 1.g6 wins.
ex.e13: Your a6-pawn is passed, but the black king on c6 watches it; you still have c4 and e3 against c7 and d6. How do you create a second passed pawn? Find the winning move.
ex.e13.hint: The black king can't look after two passed pawns on different wings. Which pawn sacrifices itself to open the way for the e-pawn?
ex.e13.solution: 1.c5! After 1...dxc5, 2.e4!, and the e-pawn runs: if 2...Kb6, 3.e5; if 2...Kxa6, 4.e6 and 5.e7, far from the king. If Black doesn't take on c5, 2.cxd6 and White has two passed pawns. 1.e4 at once allows 1...Kb6, and the king gets back in time: a draw. 1.a7 also only draws.
ex.e14: Kings on f8 and h8; your pawns on f2 and g4 against g6 and h5. Taking on h5 looks obvious. Is it? Find the winning move.
ex.e14.hint: Let the h-pawn run: what matters is clearing the way for a pawn of yours that arrives with check. The f-pawn still has a part to play.
ex.e14.solution: 1.g5! Not 1.gxh5? gxh5, and Black's h-pawn gets there first. After 1...h4, 2.f4! h3, 3.f5! gxf5 and 4.g6: the g-pawn reaches g7 with check, queens on g8 with check and the new queen captures the h-pawn. Each White move is the only one that wins.
ex.e15: Pawns on f4 and h4 against g6: the f5 breakthrough is ready. But Black has the c6-pawn, and your king is on a4. What comes first? Find the winning move.
ex.e15.hint: If you break through now, the c-pawn queens together with yours. First the king steps into the c-pawn's path, and along the squares where it doesn't get checked.
ex.e15.solution: 1.Kb3! If 1.f5? gxf5 2.h5 f4 3.h6 f3 4.h7 f2 5.h8=Q f1=Q: a draw. After 1.Kb3 c5, 2.Kc2!, 2...c4, 3.Kd1! (on d2 the pawn would give check on c3 at the wrong moment) and only then, with the king in front of the pawn, 4.f5! gxf5 5.h5, and the h-pawn queens. Five moves, each the only one that wins.
key.classic: Three pawns against three with the kings far away: White gives two pawns so the third can get through and promote. Only the right breakthrough wins.
key.afterAxb6: Black captured with the a-pawn: now White's c-pawn goes forward, and one of the two white pawns promotes.
key.afterCxb6: Black captured with the c-pawn: now White's a-pawn goes forward, and it gets through.
key.count: Count before you sacrifice: here the black king arrives one move too late, and the breakthrough still wins. With the king one square closer, it would fail.
key.capa: Capablanca against Edward Lasker, London, 1913: the white pawn advances without capturing anything, slips past the black pawn and can't be stopped.
key.order: Two pawns against one with the black king far away: first one white pawn fixes the black pawn, and only then comes the breakthrough.
key.side: The right breakthrough is the one that creates the passed pawn far from the black king, on the side it can't reach in time.
key.kingFirst: The breakthrough is ready, but it's too early: first the white king goes to hold the black pawn on the other side, and only then do the pawns advance.
key.wikiDefense: The same breakthrough on the kingside, now with Black to move: by pushing the middle pawn at the right moment, Black defuses the breakthrough and holds.
history: A breakthrough is when you give up one or two pawns on purpose to break through your opponent's pawn line and create a pawn that nobody can stop. It's one of the most beautiful weapons in pawn endings, and it comes up often: with the kings far away, a well-counted breakthrough decides the game on the spot. The secret is to count first: if the enemy king gets there in time to stop the new pawn, you've just lost material. All the great endgame manuals, such as Mark Dvoretsky's and Jesús de la Villa's, teach it. The master game in this lesson is a friendly played in London in 1913: the Cuban José Raúl Capablanca, who would later become world champion, got a pawn through without capturing anything, and Edward Lasker had to resign.
practice: Final training: White pawns on c5 and e5, Black pawns on d7, e7 and d6, and the black king on h8. Find the breakthrough and take the pawn all the way to a queen.
